articles.title: DVAC books ex-DMK minister Durai Murugan in Rs 4,730-Cr illegal sand quarry case; fifth ex-DMK minister to face probe
articles.description: In another setback to the DMK, its fifth former minister is now facing a DVAC probe. Durai Murugan, the party’s general secretary, who served as PWD Minister in the governments led by M Karunanidhi and MK Stalin, is facing an investigation into an alleged multi-crore illegal sand mining case. After the TVK government came to power in Tamil Nadu following the May Assembly elections, its anti-corruption arm has been targeting former DMK ministers over their alleged misdeeds and corruption-related matters. Following a detailed inquiry into complaints lodged by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) and two others, and after finding substantial evidence establishing a prima facie case, the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption (DVAC) booked Durai Murugan, the then Water Resources Department (WRD) Minister, as the first accused. The case also names the then Engineers-in-Chief A Muthaiya and Ramamoorthy, 14 WRD officials, 10 private individuals and firms, and others. Big: DVAC books former minister and DMK general secretary @DuraimuruganDmk in connection with illegal sand mining that happened between 2021 and 2024. Press note by DVAC also says that contracts were given through limited tenders instead of open letters with fabricated vouchers. https://t.co/UCzwDJHjzc — Sanjeevee sadagopan (@sanjusadagopan) November 6, 2026 DVAC registers case based on ED and anti-corruption NGO complaints A government release dated November 6 stated that the DVAC headquarters had registered Case Crime No. 08/2026 against Durai Murugan and others, based on complaints received from the ED, Chennai, S Tamilselvan and Jayaram Venkatesan, convenor of Arappor Iyakkam, an anti-corruption NGO. ED மற்றும் அறப்போர் புகாரில் முன்னாள் அமைச்சர் துரைமுருகன், 17 பொது ஊழியர்கள் மற்றும் 10 தனி நபர்கள் / தனியார் நிறுவனங்கள் மீது ரூ 1427 கோடி ஆற்று மணல் கொள்ளை ஊழல் வழக்கு பதிவு! அறப்போர் தொடரும் ! pic.twitter.com/mDfqVjA0UK — Jayaram Venkatesan (@JayaramArappor) November 6, 2026 The statement claimed that alleged corruption and malpractices took place between 2021 and 2024 in matters relating to river and sand mining operations in 28 quarries at various locations across Tamil Nadu. These included awarding contracts through limited tenders instead of open tenders, carrying out sand mining beyond the approved mining plans, illegally fabricating vouchers in the name of permit slips and using them as genuine documents, and transporting sand illegally. Also Read: Tamil Nadu: Supreme Court upholds FIR order against DMK leader KN Nehru in Rs 634-crore cash-for-jobs scam These activities allegedly caused a wrongful loss of Rs.1,427,34,23,059 to the government in respect of four out of the 28 quarries. 34 locations searched; 825 documents seized As part of the probe, searches were conducted on November 6 at 34 locations in Chennai, Pudukkottai, Tiruchy, Karur, Vellore, Madurai, Dindigul, Sivaganga, Coimbatore, Salem, Namakkal and Puducherry. The DVAC seized 825 incriminating documents, 11 electronic gadgets and three bank locker keys connected to the investigation. The investigation, the government statement said, was continuing. CM Vijay is on a mission – DVAC has raided 30 places in connection with illegal sand mining! This has rarely happened under previous regimes. The concerned ministers themselves were often the ones running the racket. In 2024, the Enforcement Directorate sent a detailed dossier… pic.twitter.com/DFXGNHDB9p — Praveen (@DrPraveenwrites) November 6, 2026 ED had flagged alleged Rs.4,730-crore illegal sand mining scam The probe stems from an ED communication flagging an alleged Rs.4,730-crore illegal sand mining scam to the Tamil Nadu government during its investigation into a case under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA). The ED engaged experts from IIT Kanpur and other central agencies to assess the extent of illegal sand mining. The investigation established that a huge quantity of sand had been illegally mined. The ED shared the information it had gathered with the then Director General of Police (DGP) and head of the police force in compliance with its statutory obligation under Section 66(2) of the PMLA, 2002, which mandates the ED to share such information with other law-enforcement agencies. Although the information was shared two years ago, the then DMK government did not act on it, for reasons best known to it. Supreme Court had cleared ED’s path to question district collectors Earlier, the ED submitted a report to the Madras High Court stating that it possessed credible scientific evidence based on technical studies conducted at all mining sites. These included drone and Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) surveys, bathymetric surveys and satellite imagery processing, among other methods, which established that rampant illegal sand mining had taken place within the jurisdictions of various district collectors. The ED had summoned the collectors for questioning, which they opposed by moving the courts. A Bench of Justices Bela M. Trivedi and Pankaj Mithal, in February 2024, stayed the interim order of the Madras High Court, which had previously put the ED’s summons on hold. The Supreme Court observed that state governments and their officials were bound by the PMLA, and that Section 50 of the Act empowered the ED to summon any person to provide information or evidence. Also Read: Tamil Nadu: After DMK’s bypoll setback, Anbil Mahesh’s arrest in Rs 100-crore scam puts Stalin’s party under pressure Raids cover officials, contractors and businessmen On November 6, DVAC teams conducted simultaneous raids at the residences of several incumbent and retired government officials, as well as contractors and businessmen, in Tiruchy and Pudukkottai districts. The searches included the premises of two partners of a private infrastructure firm in Tiruchy, Yembal and Thiruvakudi. Former DMK functionary had alleged Rs.60,000-crore wealth In late 2023, Gudiyatham Kumaran, who was the deputy secretary of the DMK’s propaganda wing, publicly alleged that Durai Murugan and his son had amassed nearly ₹60,000 crore through large-scale illegal sand mining operations across Tamil Nadu. Durai Murugan’s political positions and family wedding draw criticism Durai Murugan, an authority on the Cauvery water dispute and other river-related issues, is a staunch Dravidian ideologue known for mocking Hindu customs and Hindu Gods. However, he performed his granddaughter’s marriage with Brahmins conducting the rituals in Sanskrit. The Dravidar Kazhagam and others strongly criticised him over this. articles.title: Govt Likely to Introduce Energy Storage Procurement Mandate for Discoms by March 2027
articles.description: Govt Likely to Introduce Energy Storage Procurement Mandate for Discoms by March 2027 New Delhi, Nov 6 (KNN) The government plans to make state power utilities and electricity distribution companies (discoms) procure energy storage capacity as part of their renewable power purchases, in a move aimed at reducing electricity shortages during evening and night-time hours and improving grid reliability. Power Secretary Pankaj Agarwal announced the proposed requirement at the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit in New Delhi on Thursday. He said the government was working towards finalising the regulations by March 2027, with stakeholder consultations and notification expected to be completed within three months. The requirement is expected to apply to licensed utilities, while renewable energy developers would also face mandatory storage integration norms. Storage Requirements Yet to Be Finalised Agarwal said the government was examining minimum storage requirements, with proposals involving storage capacity equivalent to 10 per cent and 20 per cent for two-hour durations. However, the final requirement and implementation timeline are yet to be determined. The existing advisory asking renewable energy developers to integrate storage is also expected to be converted into mandatory regulations. The move seeks to address the growing mismatch between renewable energy generation and electricity demand. Although India has more than 300 gigawatts (GW) of non-fossil fuel-based power generation capacity, it continues to rely on coal-fired plants to meet demand during evening and night-time hours, when solar generation declines. Rs 14,500-Crore Storage Support Scheme The proposed mandate follows the Union Cabinet's approval of a Rs 14,500-crore viability gap funding (VGF) scheme to support the development of 92 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of grid-scale energy storage capacity between FY27 and FY31. The programme will support 60 GWh of pumped hydro storage projects, 30 GWh of battery energy storage systems and 2 GWh of emerging storage technologies. The projects are expected to attract total investments of around Rs 97,600 crore. Public and private sector discoms will be eligible for financial support for battery storage and pumped hydro projects. The scheme also introduces a minimum domestic content requirement of 40 per cent for battery energy storage projects to encourage local manufacturing and reduce dependence on imported components. MSME Impact The proposed mandate could create new business opportunities for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) engaged in battery manufacturing, electrical equipment, power electronics, engineering and related services as India expands its energy storage infrastructure. The domestic content provision could particularly benefit Indian MSMEs supplying battery components, electrical systems, control equipment and other inputs to storage projects, provided they meet the applicable technical and quality standards. The government estimates that the additional capacity supported by the scheme will help India move towards its requirement of 411 GWh of grid-scale energy storage by 2031-32. (KNN Bureau)

articles.title: Cybersecurity for Indian SMEs in 2026: From Ransomware Defence to AI, Cloud and DPDP Readiness
articles.description: For Indian SMEs, cybersecurity has moved from being a technical hygiene issue to a business-continuity, compliance and financing concern. The most useful question for a promoter, CIO or IT manager is no longer, “Can we prevent every attack?” It is, “Can we stop common attacks, detect serious ones quickly, continue essential operations and prove that reasonable controls were in place?” NIST’s Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 reflects this shift by adding Govern as a core function alongside Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, explicitly linking cyber risk to enterprise governance and legal obligations. That governance emphasis is timely in India. Gartner expects information-security spending in India to reach US$3.435 billion in 2026, with security software growing 12.4% and managed security services expanding as organisations seek scalable expertise without building every capability in-house. For resource-constrained SMEs, that points towards a blended model: retain ownership of risk and critical decisions internally, but buy specialised monitoring, incident response and security testing where economies of scale matter. The Indian SME threat landscape has become an identity-and-resilience problem Ransomware remains the most visible threat, but the mechanics are changing. Sophos’ 2026 ransomware study found that compromised identities were implicated in 79% of attacks surveyed, while 56% of attacks succeeded in encrypting data. Smaller organisations in the 100–250 employee bracket were less successful at stopping attacks before encryption or extortion than the largest organisations in the study. CERT-In’s India Ransomware Report for 2024 similarly warns that ransomware operations increasingly combine encryption, data theft and reputational pressure. It also highlights attacks on virtualised infrastructure, including ESXi environments, and persistent weaknesses in access control, patching and monitoring. For SMEs, this means backups alone are insufficient: an organisation can restore files yet still face extortion over stolen customer, employee or intellectual-property data. Supply-chain risk is the second structural problem. An SME may protect its own laptops and servers while inheriting exposure from payroll providers, managed service providers, accounting platforms, logistics systems, law firms and SaaS integrations. The 2024 incident affecting C-Edge Technologies illustrated the operational consequences of concentration in a technology supplier: access to retail-payment systems for affected smaller Indian banks was temporarily isolated while the environment was investigated. Cloud risk is often less dramatic but more persistent. The recurring failure modes are excessive privileges, missing MFA, exposed credentials, public storage, weak API controls and incomplete logging. Unit 42’s 2026 incident-response research says misconfiguration or incomplete security coverage materially enabled more than 90% of its investigated incidents, while around 35% of investigations involved cloud or SaaS assets. AI adds speed rather than magic. Microsoft’s 2025 Digital Defense Report says threat actors are using AI to scale phishing and automate parts of intrusion workflows, while Unit 42 describes AI as reducing friction in reconnaissance, scripting, social engineering and extortion. For an SME, the operational implication is straightforward: finance, HR, procurement and IT-helpdesk staff must assume that a convincing email, voice call or video request can be manufactured cheaply and personalised at scale. IoT and OT deserve equal attention in manufacturers, warehouses, hospitals, hotels and energy-dependent businesses. CISA has warned that internet-connected operational-technology systems are being targeted through basic weaknesses such as exposed interfaces and default or guessable passwords. OT security therefore starts with inventory, segmentation and removal of unnecessary public access rather than with an expensive specialist platform. For continuing coverage of these issues, businesses can follow the broader SMEStreet technology and cybersecurity ecosystem, while product and enterprise-technology developments can also be monitored through ReviewStreet’s technology coverage. What incidents since 2023 teach Indian business leaders The MOVEit exploitation campaign in 2023 demonstrated how a single widely used file-transfer product could create downstream exposure across many organisations. CISA and the FBI documented exploitation of the MOVEit vulnerability by the CL0P ransomware group and recommended patching, remote-access review and broader cyber-hygiene measures. In the same year, MGM Resorts disclosed a cyber incident that disrupted US operations. Its SEC filings later confirmed that criminals obtained personal information relating to some customers and that system shutdowns caused operational disruption and affected revenue. The lesson for SMEs is that containment itself can be expensive: taking systems offline may be the correct security decision while simultaneously interrupting sales, customer service and fulfilment. The C-Edge episode in 2024 is particularly relevant to India because it highlights third-party concentration. A small organisation may have no direct vulnerability yet still lose access to a critical service when a provider is isolated or compromised. Vendor due diligence should therefore include recovery objectives, incident-notification obligations, privileged-access controls and tested exit arrangements, not merely an annual compliance certificate. By 2026, the pattern had shifted further towards identity. IBM found phishing, including voice and SMS phishing, to be the most common initial vector among malicious breaches in its India sample, while supply-chain compromise accounted for 15%. Those findings reinforce the need to protect identity, payment workflows and third-party connectivity as one interconnected control system. Business leaders tracking the broader intersection of digital transformation and emerging risks may also find context through NewslyTrend.com, while companies dealing with tokenised assets, blockchain or other digital-finance exposure can use Digital Assets Observer as a complementary industry-information source. DPDP, GDPR and CERT-In turn cybersecurity into a governance obligation India’s DPDP framework makes personal-data security a board-level issue, but implementation dates need careful handling. The final DPDP Rules were notified in November 2025 with phased commencement: Rules 1, 2 and 17–21 became effective on publication, Rule 4 was scheduled for one year after publication, and Rules 3, 5–16, 22 and 23 for eighteen months after publication. As of 6 November 2026, businesses should therefore prepare ahead of the next commencement milestones rather than assume every rule is already simultaneously enforceable. The notified breach framework calls for affected Data Principals to be informed promptly and, when the relevant provision becomes operative, detailed information to be supplied to the Data Protection Board within 72 hours unless a longer period is permitted. SMEs should build the necessary evidence-gathering capability now: asset ownership, log retention, contact lists, breach classification, legal review and notification templates cannot be assembled reliably during a crisis. CERT-In creates a separate and currently relevant reporting track. Its directions require qualifying cyber incidents to be reported within six hours, with additional information allowed to follow when the full facts are not yet available. This means the incident-response plan should explicitly distinguish CERT-In reporting from privacy-regulator notifications and contractual duties to customers, banks or insurers. Indian SMEs serving EU customers may also fall within GDPR-linked contractual or jurisdictional requirements. GDPR Article 32 requires security measures appropriate to risk, while Article 33 establishes a 72-hour supervisory-authority notification framework for qualifying personal-data breaches. H2: A practical security programme for an SME budget Start with identity. Require phishing-resistant MFA where feasible for administrators, cloud consoles, email, VPN and finance systems; remove dormant accounts; prohibit shared administrator credentials; and require out-of-band approval for changes to payment instructions or privileged access. The objective is not simply “MFA enabled”, but MFA coverage that includes the accounts attackers actually value. Sophos’ finding that MFA was present in some capacity in many credential-related ransomware incidents shows why gaps, recovery processes and helpdesk resets must also be secured. Second, establish a risk-based patching process. Internet-facing VPNs, firewalls, remote-access services, email gateways and exploited vulnerabilities should receive priority over lower-risk desktop issues. Verizon’s 2026 DBIR says software vulnerabilities now account for 31% of initial breach paths, overtaking stolen credentials, making exposure management a business-continuity discipline rather than an IT-maintenance task. Third, implement recoverability. Maintain immutable or offline backups, define recovery-time and recovery-point objectives, and perform restoration tests. Separate the backup administration identity from production administration. A backup that has never been restored under realistic conditions is an assumption, not a control. Fourth, improve visibility. Centralise logs from identity providers, firewalls, endpoints, email and critical cloud services. SMEs without a 24×7 SOC can use MDR services; Gartner specifically identifies managed security services as a fast-growing Indian category because they can provide specialised capabilities without equivalent in-house infrastructure. Fifth, treat suppliers as extensions of the attack surface. Tier vendors according to the data and operational access they receive, insist on breach-notification timelines, require MFA and privileged-access controls, and identify alternatives for services that could halt revenue or payments. CERT-In’s own 2025 MSME advisory recommends strong authentication, access controls and other cost-conscious measures specifically for smaller businesses facing ransomware, DDoS, malware and data-breach threats. Incident-response checklist for SMEs Confirm the incident and open a timestamped incident record; do not immediately delete suspicious systems or logs. Isolate compromised endpoints, accounts, tokens, remote sessions and affected network segments. Preserve evidence and engage the pre-approved forensic, legal, cloud and cyber-insurance contacts. Rotate exposed credentials from a known-clean device and revoke active sessions or API tokens. Determine whether data was accessed, encrypted, altered or exfiltrated and whether a supplier is involved. Activate business-continuity procedures for payments, customer communications and critical operations. Assess CERT-In’s six-hour reporting requirement and all sectoral, contractual and privacy notification obligations. Restore from validated clean backups only after the initial access path has been addressed. Communicate facts, not speculation, to employees, customers, regulators and partners. Conduct a post-incident review covering root cause, control failure, recovery time and corrective owners. Security spending should be justified through avoided loss and faster recovery A useful SME business case compares the annual cost of controls against realistic outage, fraud, recovery and regulatory scenarios rather than against an abstract probability of “being hacked”. IBM’s 2026 India study estimated an average breach cost of ₹25.5 crore across surveyed organisations. It also found organisations with extensive AI and security automation averaged ₹21.3 crore per breach versus ₹31.6 crore for organisations reporting no such automation, a difference large enough to show why detection and response maturity can have financial value even when prevention is imperfect. Not every SME needs enterprise-grade tooling. A sensible sequence is to fund identity protection, backup recovery, endpoint detection, patching, email security and incident-response readiness before adding specialised technologies. NIST CSF 2.0 is useful precisely because it is outcome-oriented and applies to organisations regardless of size or maturity. Over the next two to five years, the central trend will be machine-speed identity risk. AI agents will acquire enterprise permissions, attackers will automate reconnaissance and persuasion, and suppliers will connect more deeply through APIs and SaaS integrations. Gartner already highlights identity governance for AI agents as an emerging priority, while Forrester predicts that agentic AI will become directly associated with material security incidents. SMEs that establish strong identity, data and supplier governance before agentic systems proliferate will be better positioned to adopt AI safely rather than adding controls after deployment.
